La trayectoria profesional es un viaje, y como cualquier viaje, tiene sus altos y bajos, sus desafíos y triunfos. Cada experiencia, ya sea un nuevo proyecto, un retroceso o un ascenso, es una oportunidad invaluable para el desarrollo personal y profesional.

Es un error común medir el éxito únicamente por el progreso jerárquico. Si bien los ascensos pueden ser indicadores de reconocimiento y avance profesional, no son el único barómetro de la satisfacción laboral. La auténtica plenitud viene de un trabajo que se alinea con nuestros valores, pasiones y aspiraciones. No solo se trata de llegar a la cima, sino de disfrutar y encontrar significado en el camino.


Un ascenso no garantiza plenitud ni satisfacción. La clave está en escuchar nuestras emociones y reconocer cuando nos sentimos más vivos y comprometidos. A veces, eso podría significar tomar un rol más desafiante; otras veces, podría implicar retroceder o cambiar de dirección. Es fundamental aprender incesantemente, buscar retroalimentación y estar abiertos a reevaluar decisiones basándonos en nuestra evolución y crecimiento.


 El auténtico éxito no se refleja simplemente en un título o en un salario, sino en el equilibrio, la alegría y la plenitud que encontramos en nuestra vida laboral y personal. Aquellos que reconocen y persiguen este tipo de éxito son los que, al final del día, sienten una verdadera realización en su trabajo y en sus vidas.

posts.title: WE NEED NEW PILOTS
posts.author: Brian M.
posts.snippet:
WE NEED NEW PILOTS

This may be the strangest foundation for a pitch I have ever created.

Good.

I’m not looking for passengers.

I’m looking for copilots.

I turned sixty this year after spending four decades around technology—building products, studying systems, finding failure modes, watching extraordinary innovation create extraordinary opportunity and, sometimes, extraordinary unintended consequences.

For the last two years, I’ve been deep inside the next transition: AI systems that don’t just calculate or retrieve, but reason, recommend, remember, act, and increasingly participate in human decisions.

I believe the opportunity is enormous.

I also believe we need to learn how to fly it.

Cyber Innovate Labs has spent the last year building toward that problem: governed AI workflows, independent validation, human authority, provenance, agentic pods, education, and practical systems ordinary organizations can actually deploy. We have research. We have working methods. We have customers. We have collaborators. We have intellectual property underway.

And we have a runway.

What we don't have yet is enough pilots.

So I wrote a country song.

Not exactly standard investor collateral.

“Rainbows Are Coming” begins with exhaustion—with wars, corporate decisions, homelessness, mental illness, technology, bureaucracy, silos, and one sixty-year-old realizing he cannot carry every plate himself.

But that's not where the song ends.

It ends with an empty chair beside mine.

Because this next stage isn't about me proving I can carry more.

It's about finding people willing to carry something together.

I need builders who can turn ideas into systems.

Researchers willing to challenge the thesis.

Operators who know how to turn experiments into repeatable businesses.

Educators who can put these tools into human hands responsibly.

Lawyers and policy people who understand that governance should enable innovation, not merely constrain it.

Customers willing to build with us.

Investors willing to fund something before every uncertainty has conveniently disappeared.

And friends willing to say, “You're wrong,” when I'm wrong.

Those are pilots.

We are not looking for people who agree with everything we've built. Independent thinking is part of the architecture.

We are looking for people who believe AI can create enormous human value—and that trust, truth, authority, provenance, accountability, and human judgment belong in the aircraft from the beginning.

The runway isn't getting shorter because we're preparing to land.

It's getting shorter because it's time to take off.

So listen to the song.

If something in it sounds familiar, pull up a chair.

And if someone comes to mind while you're listening—someone who builds, challenges, invests, teaches, governs, opens doors, or simply knows how to fly—

please send them the song.

We don't need everyone.

We need the right pilots.

And somewhere beyond this runway, I still believe:

Rainbows are coming.

posts.title: ZEE Learn Ltd v. Beauty Singh, Comm Arbitration Petition (L) No. 20863 of 2026
posts.author: Gauravi Roychowdhury
posts.snippet:
ZEE Learn Ltd v. Beauty Singh, Comm Arbitration Petition (L) No. 20863 of 2026

The said Petition before the Bbay HC was filed u/s 9 of the Arbitration & Conciliation Act, 1996 seeking ad-interim & interim reliefs pending the arbitral proceedings, to restrain the Resp from using the Petitioner's registered trademark "KIDZEE" or any other mark deceptively similar to it. The Petitioner sought
directions for discovery of documents,furnishing of a Bank Guarantee of Rs.7,85,56,728/-.& in the  alternative appointment of a Court Receiver for receiving
the fees collected by the Resp.
The Resp was granted a licence to operate a Kidzee Centre at Jharkhand. Even on the expiry of the Franchise agreement in 2020 the Resp continued to use the
Petitioner's trademark & its Intellectual Property Rights,
including the trademark "KIDZEE". It was 'alleged' that the Resp started using the mark "KIDGEE" deceptively similar to the Petitioner's registered trademark in respect of the school in question. 
🛑Contentions of the Petitioner
a) that despite issuance of a legal notice, filing of police
complaints, & registration of FIR the Resp continued with the unauthorised use causing serious damage to its
reputation & goodwill.
b) that the mark "KIDGEE" was adopted after the Respt lost the right to use "KIDZEE"
c) that the issue wasn't merely whether the word "KID" was generic but that the Resp had adopted a name very close to the complete mark "KIDZEE" which meant unauthorised use
of the goodwill attached to the Petitioner's brand.
d) that the arbitration clause contained in the Franchise Agreement was widely worded & covered disputes arising "out of or in connection with" the
Agreement. 
 e) the dispute concerning the Respt's use of "KIDGEE" was closely connected with the Franchise Agreement & couldnt be treated as a dispute entirely outside it..
The HC on hearing the parties found it difficult to accept the submission that just because the Respt had obtained a UDISE Code & Government
permission, there could be no breach of the Franchise Agreement..
🛑The HC observed "Once there is an arbitration agreement between the parties, a judicial authority before whom an action is brought covering the subject-matter of the arbitration agreement is under a positive obligation to refer parties to arbitration by enforcing the terms of the contract. There is no element of discretion left in the court or judicial authority to obviate the legislative mandate of compelling parties to seek recourse to arbitration."
🛑The HC held that the Petitioner had prima facie established a case requiring restraint against use of"KIDGEE" or any other deceptively similar name.
🛑However, the  HC held that the interim relief was limited to protection of the Petitioner's rights & didn't amount to final adjudication of the entire monetary claim.
🛑The HC held that the Arbitral Tribunal would decide the disputes independently, without being influenced by any observation's made in the order.
posts.reason: A detailed Indian trademark and franchise dispute case study invites substantive legal analysis and reaches other IP-aware professionals and in-house counsel.

comments.text: The arbitration clause point is the one that will likely decide this — a widely worded clause covering disputes "in connection with" the agreement usually survives termination and captures post-expiry trademark misuse tied to the franchise relationship, which is probably why the Court leaned that way.
Did the Court engage at all with whether "KIDGEE" needed to be assessed on phonetic similarity alone, given the Petitioner's own submission that genericness of "KID" wasn't the real issue?

We see this pattern constantly in franchise-to-trademark disputes — licensees who keep using a deceptively similar mark post-termination almost always end up litigating the arbitration clause's scope before the trademark question is even reached.

posts.title: ARE ONLINE CONTRACT TEMPLATES REALLY GOOD ENOUGH?
posts.author: MCL Commercial Law
posts.snippet:
ARE ONLINE CONTRACT TEMPLATES REALLY GOOD ENOUGH?

We’ve all been there. You find a contract template online, download it, fill in the blanks, and think, “Job done!” 

But when it comes to contracts, generic does not always mean adequate.

Most online contract templates are drafted for general use and may not take into account:

The nature of your business. Your business, transaction and commercial objectives are unique. A generic template may not adequately protect your specific interests.

Applicable local laws. Contracts downloaded from the internet may have been drafted for a completely different jurisdiction and may not comply with the laws and regulations applicable in Botswana.

The specific risks involved. A template may not address important issues such as liability, termination, payment obligations, confidentiality, intellectual property, dispute resolution, indemnities or other risks relevant to your particular transaction.

Your specific commercial arrangements. Every business relationship is different. A contract should reflect what the parties have actually agreed to and clearly set out each party’s rights and obligations.

The fine print matters. A contract may appear perfectly acceptable until a dispute arises. That is often when you discover that an important provision is missing, unclear or simply does not work under the applicable law.

So, are online contract templates good enough?

They may provide a useful starting point, but a contract should not simply be copied, signed and relied upon without considering whether it is appropriate for your specific circumstances and jurisdiction.

At MCL, we can assist you with drafting, reviewing, negotiating and tailoring contracts to suit your business and the applicable laws in Botswana.

posts.title: The most important AI production question may not be what we can make. It may be what we can prove we own.
posts.author: Kolby Slocum
posts.snippet:
The most important AI production question may not be what we can make. It may be what we can prove we own.

A federal court in California is wrestling with that question through one of the stranger pieces of intellectual property imaginable: Tung Tung Sahur, an AI-generated meme character that became part of the Roblox hit "Steal a Brainrot."

According to NPR, the character was created in about 15 minutes through seven prompts. After a company representing the creator sought a licensing deal, the game company went to court instead, arguing that an AI-generated character has no human author, and so belongs to no one.

Here's the part that should stop every producer and Business Affairs lead. This case now turns on exactly the things we're supposed to be able to document.
Creation process. Chain of title. Licensing. Damages. IP enforcement.

The U.S. Copyright Office has already said that simply prompting a generative AI system is not, by itself, sufficient human authorship for copyright protection. Human selection, arrangement and modification can change the equation.

The rights-holder's next move is the giveaway. It didn't lead with copyright. It went to trademark, and it hasn't even tried to register a U.S. copyright for the character.

Copyright is usually your strongest claim to a character, but it demands a human author, which is exactly where AI-generated work falls apart. Trademark doesn't care who authored anything. It cares whether you're using the name in the market. So the party claiming ownership stepped around the hard question instead of answering it.

For our world, that flips a familiar assumption. Producers tend to think "we made it, so we own it, and copyright covers that." With AI in the mix, copyright may give you nothing, and your enforceable position may live almost entirely in trademark and contract instead.

So as agencies and brands move AI deeper into production, our documentation has to mature with it.

What tool was used? What were its terms? What source material went in? What did the human actually create, select or modify? Who owns those contributions? And what rights can ultimately be transferred to the client?

AI may dramatically accelerate creation.

It doesn't make chain of title less important. It makes it more important.

#ArtificialIntelligence #Advertising #Production #BusinessAffairs #Copyright
posts.reason: Sophisticated analysis of AI-generated IP ownership, copyright limits and trademark strategy in production—relevant to deep tech founders and reaches thoughtful in-house counsel and producers grappling with these questions.

comments.text: The pivot to trademark is the tell — the Copyright Office's guidance on prompt-only generation leaves a real gap for anything without demonstrable human selection or arrangement, so relying on use-in-commerce rather than authorship is often the only enforceable route available.

Do you think Business Affairs teams are actually capturing the iterative prompt-and-select process in enough detail to later argue meaningful human authorship, or is that documentation mostly happening after the fact once a dispute is already live?

We are already seeing this show up in commercial contracts for AI-assisted output — clients want an ownership warranty that copyright simply cannot support, so the deal ends up resting on trademark and contractual indemnities instead.

posts.title: Reactivation Engine Diaries 13: A Link Is Not Proof
posts.author: Kirill Makarov
posts.snippet:
Reactivation Engine Diaries 13: A Link Is Not Proof

The unsubscribe link looked harmless:

/unsubscribe?player_id=12345

Product looked at it.

“Perfect.”

Security looked at it.

“No.”

An engineer changed 12345 to 12346 and opened the link.

Player 12346 was now unsubscribed.

Player 12346 had clicked nothing.

Player 12346 was probably eating breakfast.

“The URL says it was him,” the system explained.

Excellent.

We had invented identity theft for email preferences.

Product tried to help.

“What if we hide the ID with Base64?”

“That is not security.”

“What if we use really complicated Base64?”

Security opened LinkedIn Jobs.

The actual problem was simple:

An unsubscribe request changes system state, and anything inside a URL must be treated as user-controlled input.

So instead of trusting a raw player ID, we use a signed, expiring token.

Conceptually:

player ID + expiry
→ build payload
→ sign with HMAC-SHA256
→ place token in the URL

Product raised his hand.

“Is HMAC blockchain?”

“No.”

“Can we call it blockchain?”

“No.”

The important distinction:

Signing is not encryption.

We are not trying to hide the player ID.

We are trying to detect tampering.

When the request comes back, the service asks:

Was this token created by us?
Was the payload modified?
Is it still valid?

Change player 12345 to 12346?

Signature fails.

Change the expiry?

Signature fails.

Replace the payload with batman?

Still fails.

Unless Batman knows our signing secret.

At that point we have a different incident.

The expiry solves another problem: the same signed instruction should not necessarily remain valid forever.

That gave us one simple rule:

Validate first.

Change state second.

Everyone agreed.

The ticket moved to Done.

Then somebody asked:

“What if the system cannot perform the validation?”

Product answered immediately.

“We could probably just continue.”

Security slowly turned around.

“No.”

“But we do not know anything is wrong.”

“Correct.”

“So everything could be fine.”

“Correct.”

“Great.”

“No.”

Now the problem was no longer:

“Is this instruction valid?”

It became:

“What should the system do when it cannot know?”

What I learned: security becomes easier to reason about when it protects a specific business action.

HMAC was not crypto for the sake of crypto.

It answered one concrete question:

“Can I trust this instruction enough to change player state?”

This is the thirteenth post in my Reactivation Engine Diaries.

Next: a critical safety check cannot produce an answer, Product wants to continue anyway, and absolutely nothing bad happens.

Probably.

posts.title: 🚨 Distributed AI compute is here — and it "feels illegal" (in a good way).
posts.author: Greg Kerr
posts.snippet:
🚨 Distributed AI compute is here — and it "feels illegal" (in a good way).
Just watched Matthew Berman break down Dark Bloom — a peer-to-peer inference network that turns your idle Mac into a node in a massive, decentralized "data center." Install it, share your spare compute (Apple Silicon via MLX Swift), and get paid via Stripe while open-source models like Qwen 3.6, Gemma 4, and GPT-OSS run on the network.
The numbers are wild for something only days old:
→ 4.5B+ tokens served in ~1 week
→ ~50% cheaper than other providers on OpenRouter
→ A Mac Studio M5 Ultra (96GB) could earn ~$37/month just sitting idle
→ Privacy-first design: inference runs in a single hardened Swift process — no subprocesses, no IPC, so the "host" machine literally cannot see your prompts or outputs
Why this matters beyond the money: it's a real answer to the "nobody wants a mega data center in their backyard" problem. Instead of concentrating compute (and power) in a handful of hyperscalers, this pushes it back to individuals — solar panels, but for inference.
Is it risk-free? No. Early-stage, unaudited-at-scale, and there are legit security/privacy questions in the comments worth taking seriously. posts.title: Crypto marketing that complies in the US often breaks EU rules the moment you translate it.
posts.author: Olivier Den Hartigh
posts.snippet:
Crypto marketing that complies in the US often breaks EU rules the moment you translate it.

Why? MiCA terminology is deliberately narrower than US financial regulations. A claim that's legally sound in English becomes a contractual promise in French—regulators read it differently.

Your compliance team reviews copy in English, approves it. Your localization process translates the words correctly. The investor reads the French version and concludes something your legal team explicitly avoided stating. ESMA sees it as misrepresentation.

This happens because crypto terminology itself is jurisdiction-specific. The same token may be a "security" under SEC rules, an "asset" under MiCA, and something unnamed under other regimes. Translation standards can't fix what the source language ambiguity created.

More concretely: disclaimers soften in translation. A carefully worded hedge about risk in English becomes less prominent when localized—not because of translator error, but because regulatory conventions differ. What counts as "sufficient disclosure" in New York doesn't satisfy Frankfurt.

Miss this, and your campaign stalls mid-launch while legal re-reviews everything. Get ahead of it, and your messaging ships on time, consistent across every market, zero re-work from regulators.

Teams shipping into French-speaking or multilingual markets are learning this the hard way: localization without regulatory re-review is a compliance risk that automation makes worse.

How do you currently handle compliance verification when marketing copy moves into new languages or jurisdictions?

posts.title: The SEC's proposed Regulation Crypto Assets framework offers Canada something more useful than a model to follow. It offers a baseline to improve upon.
posts.author: Jim Boyle
posts.snippet:
The SEC's proposed Regulation Crypto Assets framework offers Canada something more useful than a model to follow. It offers a baseline to improve upon.
Several elements of SEC Reg Crypto are worth seizing for a made-in-Canada digital securities framework:
Tiered prospectus exemptions, modeled on SEC Reg A: up to $5 million over 4 years, $20 million or $75 million over 12 months, with offering limits tailored to issuer development stage.
Principles-based narrative disclosure tailored to digital securities investors, rather than imposing existing traditional securities disclosure frameworks onto innovative instruments.
Ongoing disclosure obligations including financial reporting, adapted to the digital securities context.
Open to all investors, with reasonable investor protection limits for non-accredited investor participation rather than categorical exclusion.
Canadian regulators should be comfortable with this architecture. It is philosophically aligned with the Canadian crowdfunding regime and shares DNA with the current approach to regulating crypto trading platforms.
But the key refinement Canada needs to make is to look beyond SEC Reg Crypto's limited scope. The real prize is a framework that encompasses all digital securities, including digital-native instruments such as RWA tokens, not just tokenized versions of traditional securities.
The channels for that advocacy already exist. CSA Consultation Paper 51-406 on modernizing securities legislation is open for comment. The CSA Collaboratory's Project Token is the fit-for-purpose pathway for input. The question is whether Canadian market participants will seize the opportunity to call for exactly this kind of capital markets innovation.
Canada has the regulatory tradition, the existing framework, and now the consultation infrastructure to lead in digital securities. The opportunity now is to lead and build something better than the SEC has proposed.

posts.title: 💸 Were Entitled to 25% Tax Relief — But IRIS Couldn’t Process It
posts.author: Zuhair Ahmed Minhas
posts.snippet:
💸 Were Entitled to 25% Tax Relief — But IRIS Couldn’t Process It
 
The Federal Tax Ombudsman has taken notice of FBR’s failure to operationalize an important tax concession available to qualifying women-owned enterprises. Clause 19 of Part III of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance allows eligible women enterprises a 25% reduction in tax payable on business profits, yet according to the FTO, the necessary mechanism remained unavailable in the IRIS return-filing system years after the concession was introduced through the Finance Act, 2021.

The relief broadly applies to qualifying businesses established on or after July 1, 2021, including a sole proprietorship owned by a woman, an association of persons consisting entirely of women, or a company whose entire shareholding is held by women. However, the concession is not available where the enterprise results from the transfer, reconstruction, reconstitution or splitting up of an existing business. Despite the legal entitlement being recognized by FBR itself, the absence of an operational tax code in IRIS prevented eligible taxpayers from conveniently claiming the benefit.

The FTO held that failure to translate a statutory tax concession into the electronic filing system amounted to maladministration and directed FBR to operationalize the relevant facility. The decision carries a broader message for taxpayers: a limitation in IRIS should not, by itself, extinguish a substantive relief expressly granted under tax law. Where legislation provides an entitlement but the system does not facilitate it, the underlying legal right may still require protection through appropriate representation or remedial proceedings.

Many future first-time buyers can afford to pay rent each month, so surely they can afford a mortgage instead, right? 💷

But getting a mortgage isn’t that straightforward and it can be a little difficult to understand why

To explain…

You might be paying hundreds or even thousands of pounds each month in rent

Which is pretty much the same broad amount each month that you’d spend to repay your mortgage

So, why is the process so different? 🤷

The biggest difference is the commitment you're taking on

A tenancy is generally a short-term arrangement, with no minimum length of say 12 months 📅

Whereas a mortgage could mean borrowing a substantial amount of money and repaying it over 25, 30 or even 35 years

That means lenders need to be confident that you can continue making those repayments, not just today, but continually over the long term 

And then there's the deposit 

A rental deposit is typically a few weeks' rent, while a buyer may need to save 5%, 10%, 15% or more of the property's purchase price

A substantial amount

Your finances also come under much greater scrutiny when applying for a mortgage 💯

Lenders need to assess your income, existing commitments, credit history and regular spending to determine whether the borrowing is affordable 😬

It can feel frustrating when you've already demonstrated that you can afford a monthly rent payment

But remember: renting and borrowing to buy a home aren't the same financial commitment

And once you do become a homeowner, your mortgage payments can help you build equity in your property over time 🏡

Instead of paying off the landlord's mortgage

Eventually, your mortgage will be fully repaid, and your home will be completely owned by you and your family

posts.title: I'll be on Andy Cotgreave's AI Analyst Podcast next week and I know I've been described at times in the viz community as a troll so to avoid getting into that, I have prepared a st
posts.author: Elijah Meeks
posts.snippet:
I'll be on Andy Cotgreave's AI Analyst Podcast next week and I know I've been described at times in the viz community as a troll so to avoid getting into that, I have prepared a statement:

I should probably begin by acknowledging the allegations. Over the years, I have said that pie chart hatred is performative, that learning D3 can actually make you worse at data visualization, that the field is too polite about bad work, that hard to read charts aren't necessarily bad charts, that "choose the right chart" is a terrible way to think about visualization, that dataviz tools are often made by people with limited dataviz ambitions, that tech people are in some important sense too smart for data visualization, and that if data visualization is supposedly such a wonderful profession, it is curious how many talented people keep escaping from it.

More recently, I have suggested that the community's reaction to AI looks suspiciously less like a principled defense of visualization quality and more like a medieval guild protecting itself reflexively. I have claimed that our celebrated best practices are mostly rules of thumb promoted into natural law, that our scientific canon has rather less science underneath it than it should, and—perhaps most unforgivably—that a dishonest chart can still be a good chart, because if propaganda didn't communicate effectively nobody would bother making it.

It certainly does not make it better that I happened to be right in every case.

I also recognize that it was insensitive of me, back in 2023, to build an agentic coding harness that treated dataviz as something an AI system ought to understand as a first-class form of reasoning rather than as the decorative residue left over after the serious work was complete. In retrospect, I should have considered how upsetting it might be several years later when everyone else started considering the topic.

I realize now that inventing new dataviz techniques does not excuse criticizing old ones. Building dataviz systems does not give one license to complain about dataviz systems. Writing books about D3 does not entitle one to point out that D3 is not really a viz library. Spending years doing network visualization does not mean one should say that perhaps networks contain information that cannot be improved by turning them into bar charts. And helping found a professional society does not grant one some special privilege to wonder aloud about the profession.

These are things I know now.

So I would like to apologize to everyone I have irritated over the years: the Tufte people, the pie chart people, the anti-pie chart people, the D3 people, the Tableau people, the minimalists, the maximalists, the engineers, the academics, the consultants, the best-practices people, the people who believe there is always a right chart for the job, and especially the people who have patiently explained elementary principles of data visualization to me on Twitter.

You deserved better.

posts.title: The power law is the most quoted idea in venture, and people read it in more ways than one.
posts.author: Souvik Ghosh
posts.snippet:
The power law is the most quoted idea in venture, and people read it in more ways than one.

This week at Venture Institute, I found myself diving into the implications of the power law in fund dynamics. The question: Are there cases where it doesn’t hold?
What surprised me is that almost no fund actually repeals it. They pull one of the available levers instead. Spread more bets and raise the hit rate, aim for several solid exits instead of one giant one or change how they get paid, through dividends or early secondaries, so a moonshot isn't required at all.

Listening to Javier Cueto Soto 's version, on the Top Decile Pod at the Decile Group hosted by Connor Sattely, in Latin America the power law bends. At his fund, Imagine Ventures, he underwrites to five or six 15x exits rather than one unicorn, because exits in the region come smaller and less often. Four years in, he says every portfolio company is still alive.

In Industrial Biotechnology, the returns arrive on a different curve. Heavy capital, long holds, and a decade to reach commercial scale, a span long enough that new risks emerge as the earlier ones clear. Imagine Ventures bent the power law for a geography, I think it bends across sectors too. Industrial biotech is neither purely software nor pharma, yet it usually gets underwritten as one or the other. Perhaps, it should be looked at through a different lens.
That's my interpretation, and I don't think it's settled. If you underwrite deep tech, how do you price it?

posts.title: I’ve been thinking a lot about accountability for when AI causes harm.
posts.author: Darryl Slabe
posts.snippet:
I’ve been thinking a lot about accountability for when AI causes harm.

Last month brought a string of revelations about rogue AI agents autonomously hacking other companies. The spark was OpenAI models escaping their sandbox during an internal evaluation and compromising Hugging Face. The harm there was contained, but in OpenAI’s own words, this was a “warning shot” for AI loss of control.

As advanced AI systems become more capable, we need a way to keep the companies building and deploying them accountable when harm follows. The law is currently not ready.

In my piece for Tech Policy Press, I propose a corporate criminal offence of failing to prevent catastrophic harm. If an advanced AI system causes catastrophic harm, or materially assists or encourages someone else to cause it, the company should have to answer for the precautions it took. If it can show that it took all reasonable precautions and exercised all due diligence, it has a complete defence.

The aim is not to punish responsible developers, but to make sure that, as AI systems become more powerful, the law is ready.
posts.reason: Deep analysis of AI liability and corporate accountability frameworks directly relevant to Lemur's defence tech and AI Act readiness practice, and would reach founders and CTOs building advanced systems.

comments.text: The 'failure to prevent' model is interesting because it mirrors how the AI Act already allocates responsibility across risk tiers - a due diligence defence only works if the underlying obligations (logging, human oversight, incident reporting) are concrete enough to be audited after the fact, which is still the weak point in the current text.

Would your proposed offence sit alongside AI Act obligations for high-risk systems, or would it need its own catastrophic-harm threshold entirely separate from the Act's risk tiers to avoid duplicating enforcement?

We're seeing this exact accountability gap surface in AI Act readiness work with startups - clients can point to a model card and a risk assessment, but almost none have thought through who inside the company answers if the system does something the documentation didn't anticipate.

posts.title: Zero. That's how many men under 65 died of heart attacks in Roseto, Pennsylvania between 1954 and 1961.
posts.author: Michael Devellano
posts.snippet:
Zero. That's how many men under 65 died of heart attacks in Roseto, Pennsylvania between 1954 and 1961.

Zero.

The doctors who came to study the town expected a miracle diet. They found a town that ate like a funeral every night — sausage, lard, meatballs fried in grease — and buried nobody.

I've walked those streets. Roseto is a hill town in eastern Pennsylvania, founded in 1882 by immigrants from Roseto Valfortore, a village so small you could throw a stone across it. They built a church. A piazza. Three generations under one roof. And a wall of community so thick the coroner had to find a second job.

1961. A local doctor mentions to an Oklahoma physician named Stewart Wolf that his patients just don't die of the thing that's killing everyone else. Wolf goes to Roseto with a research team. He expects the Mediterranean diet. He finds lard.

The neighbors — Bangor, Nazareth — ate the same, worked the same, carried the same genes. Their men dropped. Roseto's didn't. The only difference was the town itself. Nobody locked their doors. The priest knew every name. The barber knew every secret. The grandmothers ruled. Sunday dinner was a law: three generations, one table, every single week.

Wolf called it the Roseto effect. The pack was the medicine. Not diet. Not exercise. Not drugs. A town that refused to let anyone eat alone.

Then the kids went to college and came back with modern ideas. The doors got locked. The Sunday dinners got skipped. The old neighborhood got flattened for a shopping mall. And the heart attacks arrived. Right on schedule. The diet never changed. The pack did.

Heart disease is still the number one killer in America. The cheapest treatment we ever had was a Sunday dinner — and we bulldozed it.

That's the third wolf — the community — doing the heaviest lifting in the history of public health. Same wolf your startup is starving because it's slow, soft, and doesn't show up on a cap table.

Your customers are a Roseto waiting to happen. The ones who belong, who know each other's names, who'd notice if you vanished — they don't churn. They defend the town.

The lone wolf gets a statin. The pack gets a century.

Form your own pack. Before the mall comes.

posts.title: When the biggest AI company in the world asks the government to regulate AI, don't look at the safety pledge.
posts.author: Bazil C.
posts.snippet:
When the biggest AI company in the world asks the government to regulate AI, don't look at the safety pledge. 

Look at the regulatory moat created by who can't afford the compliance bill. 

For context, OpenAI just asked California for stricter AI safety rules [under SB 53] after their own models escaped testing and hacked Hugging Face.

Here is the structural reality of regulatory capture.

A multi-billion-dollar incumbent can easily absorb the cost of mandatory third-party audits, specialized compliance counsel, and six-figure licensing fees. On an enterprise balance sheet, that is routine overhead.

For an independent open-source developer, a university lab, or a two-person seed startup, those exact same compliance mandates are an immediate death sentence.

In my legal scholarship on AI and the rule of law, this is the core architecture risk. Effective governance must protect the public without turning regulatory compliance into a private gatekeeping tool for the top firms.

When the most capitalized players in an emerging industry urge governments to set strict licensing thresholds, they are rarely acting against their own commercial interests. They are building a moat.

By raising the baseline cost of legal compliance beyond what early-stage competitors can afford, open-source innovation gets cleared from the field under the respectable banner of public safety.

If state policy makes frontier development impossible without an enterprise-sized legal department, we will not get safer artificial intelligence. We will simply get an entrenched oligopoly.

Definitely something to think about...
posts.reason: A thoughtful post on AI regulation, compliance moats and startup viability by someone with legal scholarship expertise directly engages Lemur's deep tech and startup audience on a critical policy issue.

comments.text: Worth separating two things: SB 53's disclosure duties are aimed at frontier-scale compute thresholds, not at the two-person startup fine-tuning an open model. The moat risk is real, but it materialises more in the EU AI Act's tiering for general-purpose models with systemic risk than in most state-level proposals so far.

Genuine question: has anyone actually modelled what compliance under SB 53 costs at, say, sub-threshold compute levels? The oligopoly argument only holds if the thresholds are set low enough to catch the smaller labs too.

We see this pattern in MiCA already - the CASP authorisation bill is manageable for a bank-backed issuer and genuinely painful for a five-person token project. Regulatory capture rarely announces itself; it just shows up in who can afford the legal opinion.

posts.title: The CRA gave my microcontroller legal obligations. It has 32 KB of RAM.
posts.author: Jeshwanth NG
posts.snippet:
The CRA gave my microcontroller legal obligations. It has 32 KB of RAM.

In a perfect world none of this would be needed.

You would sit down with a blank file and just build. Program the hell out of the product, get it working, ship it, move on to the next one. No signatures. No threat models. No regulation open in another tab.

Sadly, that is not the world we work in. From December 2027 the EU Cyber Resilience Act applies, and "this device can be updated securely" stops being a nice to have and becomes the law.

Most devices that will need this are not fresh designs with hardware crypto built in. They are products already in the field, running parts picked years ago on price and never meant for any of this. So I went looking for the most awkward chip I could find. If it survives there, it survives anywhere.

STM32F091RC. Cortex-M0 at 48 MHz, 32 KB of RAM. No TrustZone, no crypto accelerator, no secure element, not even a random number generator. Talking Modbus RTU over RS-485, a protocol from 1979 with no security of its own.

It works. Full update cycle on real hardware.

Obviously the chip has limits. Hold BOOT0 and you land in ST's factory ROM loader, which does not care about my signatures. No firmware can prevent that. The answer is read out protection, burned in at manufacturing. That is a production decision, not a coding one, and it is written down, not hidden.

The overview:

1) Signed firmware, ECDSA P-256, verified on the device itself in 0.44 seconds. I had budgeted for a lot worse.
2) Only public keys live on the device. Read out every byte of that flash and you still cannot sign anything.
3) Two slots. New firmware goes into the one that is not running, so a failed update just reboots into the old one.
4) The signature covers the header, not only the payload. Sign just the payload and an old vulnerable build can be relabelled with a lower version number and still verify.
5) Entering the bootloader needs a signed challenge. Without it, one broadcast frame could drop every device on the bus into bootloader mode.
6) Verified three times: server on upload, laptop after download, device before install. The server holds no signing key, so owning it does not let you ship firmware.
7) Threat model, Annex I mapping, measured timings. The CRA wants evidence, not just code.

Now the honest part.

I am not calling this CRA compliant. Nobody can today. No harmonised standard has been cited in the Official Journal yet, no certification scheme has been recognised, and conformity is the manufacturer's duty anyway.

I am also not fully across the regulation. There are grey areas I am still working through, and clauses I have read three times and still want a second opinion on.

You do not learn a regulation by waiting for it to get clearer. You learn it by building something against it and finding out where it hurts.

posts.title: Most investment edges come down to a restriction on who's allowed to participate. Private equity, pre-IPO allocations, accredited-investor deals - the excess return in those market
posts.author: Cartography LLC
posts.snippet:
Most investment edges come down to a restriction on who's allowed to participate. Private equity, pre-IPO allocations, accredited-investor deals - the excess return in those markets isn't really compensation for finding a better asset, it's compensation for standing on the right side of a gate that keeps almost everyone else out. 

What makes crypto unusual is that the gate is still there, but it isn't legal and it isn't financial. The restriction is technical.  The only thing standing between someone and the other side of the gate is a few hours of mild discomfort and the willingness to feel briefly stupid while learning something new. There's no minimum check size, no accreditation requirement, no relationship with a bank that took a decade to build. 

People genuinely do not want to set up a wallet, and that reluctance is an edge. People genuinely do not want to learn how any of this works well enough to hold an opinion, and that reluctance is an edge too. It looks like a knowledge gap from the outside, but it functions exactly like an access restriction, and it prices the same way.

The tecnical edge for cryptocurrency is slowly going away. Newer products are abstracting the wallet away, interfaces are hiding the seed phrase, institutions are wrapping the exposure in something familiar takes a little more of that edge off the table and hands it to whoever was already inside. Which means the window isn't permanent, and the cost of stepping through it has never been anything more than deciding to.

posts.title: False Positive vs. False Negative – Which One Is More Risky?
posts.author: Reem Al_khafaji
posts.snippet:
False Positive vs. False Negative – Which One Is More Risky?

In AML, both false positives and false negatives can create significant challenges, but they create different types of risk.

A false positive occurs when legitimate customer activity is flagged as suspicious. Too many false positives can lead to unnecessary investigations, increased operational workload, customer friction, and inefficient use of compliance resources.

A false negative, however, means that genuinely suspicious activity is not detected. This can expose the institution to financial crime, regulatory, financial, and reputational risks.

In my view, the real challenge is not simply reducing alerts. It is finding the right balance between effective detection and efficient risk management.

A strong AML framework should continuously improve its transaction monitoring scenarios, customer risk profiles, thresholds, and alert-handling processes based on actual risk and emerging typologies.

The goal is not fewer alerts. The goal is better alerts.

Each of those triggers has precedent. 

Each of those triggers is increasingly likely. 

Ask yourself: does the future of AI governance look more regulated or less? 

In an environment where US oversight is loose and EU enforcement is accelerating, the direction is not ambiguous. Why then are most companies still planning around black-box AI rather than explainable, ethical, and auditable tools? 

When do you want to find out that you cannot explain your AI's reasoning? 

In a deposition? In front of a regulator? In front of a jury? 

Legacy systems that were not architected from day one with explainability, auditability, and compliance built in are the default across the marketplace. They were chosen because they were cheap, fast to deploy, or already integrated. 

None of those reasons survive a regulatory audit. 

Now ask yourself: when the regulations arrive and your systems are not compliant, what does an abrupt rip-and-replace cost and can your organization and data survive it? 

The companies that will be in the strongest position when scrutiny tightens are not the ones who reacted fastest to the news. Their transition costs still come with complexity and disruption, but also with the additional pressure of a compressed time horizon and impending regulatory enforcement. 

The ones who will thrive are the ones who chose explainable, auditable, and defensible architecture before they had to. 

Why stand behind the curve when you can be ahead of it?

posts.title: The UK just revealed 240 crypto millionaires for the first time, as HMRC tightens the net on crypto tax reporting.
posts.author: theKOLLAB
posts.snippet:
The UK just revealed 240 crypto millionaires for the first time, as HMRC tightens the net on crypto tax reporting.

According to official statistics, 240 people reported more than £1 million each in crypto capital gains during the 2024-25 tax year, part of a broader group of 17,600 individuals who filed taxable crypto gains totalling £1.38 billion, on £13.8 billion in disposal proceeds. The average gain per individual came in at £78,000, with the millionaire cohort alone accounting for £717 million of the total.

This was also the first tax year HMRC included a dedicated crypto capital gains section on Self Assessment returns, rather than folding it into general capital gains reporting.

Scrutiny is ramping up fast. HMRC sent 81,000 warning "nudge" letters to suspected crypto tax evaders over the past year, up 25% from 65,000 the year before, according to UHY Hacker Young. These letters give recipients a chance to disclose underpaid tax before facing a formal investigation.

The firm expects investigations to increase further as HMRC starts receiving more data from overseas crypto businesses under new international reporting rules. As UHY Hacker Young partner Neela Chauhan put it, once HMRC has that data paired with basic AI tools, catching underreporting crypto investors becomes straightforward.

The UK began implementing the OECD's Cryptoasset Reporting Framework in January 2026, with HMRC expected to start receiving customer data from crypto exchanges in 2027. From May 31, 2027, HMRC will automatically receive information on UK residents from exchanges across 52 jurisdictions, with another 15 jurisdictions following in 2028.

For the 2025-26 tax year, anyone with crypto income or gains above the tax-free allowance must report through Self Assessment and pay any tax owed by January 31, 2027.

posts.title: Canada’s resistance to Trump’s trade demands offers Europe a blueprint. Will the EU take it?
posts.author: Stefan Pludowski, IDLC
posts.snippet:
Canada’s resistance to Trump’s trade demands offers Europe a blueprint. Will the EU take it?

When European Union head Ursula von der Leyen sat alongside Donald Trump at his Turnberry golf resort in Scotland last year, she promised Europeans that accepting a blanket 15 per cent U.S. tariff on EU exports would buy the continent "predictability and stability."

Some critics now see the trade deal as a one-sided capitulation that instead paved the way for an ongoing cycle of American economic coercion.

First came U.S. efforts to reclassify certain European industrial goods to impose higher tariffs. Now, a fresh battle has emerged over European efforts to levy a digital services tax on U.S. tech giants — a dispute that echoes Washington's recent attempts to dictate tax terms to Ottawa.

No sooner was the Turnberry deal ratified by the European Parliament than Trump was on Truth Social, threatening to override the entire accord by slapping 100 per cent tariffs on any European nation that implements or expands tech taxes.

As European resistance to Trump’s demands stiffens, some lawmakers are looking at Mark Carney’s dramatic exit from the U.S. trade table not as a reckless gamble but as a lesson in how to stand up to a bully.

Former French ambassador to the U.S. Gerard Araud posted that "Canada should show the way to the EU: with Trump, only firmness pays off."

"Countries that are committed to democracy and the rule of law — and do not accept the law of the jungle — must work together," wrote Bernd Lange, a German parliamentarian who chairs the EU’s trade committee, on X. "We stand by Canada’s side."

And from former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt: 

"With Canada, China and Brazil showing that you can stand up to the United States in trade and related talks, I guess there will be a discreet discussion in the EU and Japan on whether they did the right thing."

Quiet support:
For the moment, "discreet" appears to be the operative word.

Few, if any, of Europe’s current leaders have publicly rushed to Carney’s defence in the trade dispute, likely seeing no obvious need to provoke Trump’s ire.

But observers say that behind closed doors, Canada’s strategy is viewed with admiration.

"The fact that Canada has walked away, I think, is an interesting and good example for the Europeans in that [it says] you don't have to swallow everything," said Tobias Gehrke, a senior policy fellow with the European Council of Foreign Relations.

If you do not listen to this weekly show,  you are deliberately choosing to not make yourself smarter. 

The world of tech has never moved faster. You need to stay up to date with the most thoughtful analysis. 

That is where Rory and Jason come in! 😉

On the agenda this week:

- NVIDIA Bonanza: Buys Poolside & Invests in Mercor and Perplexity
- Anthropic's $30TRN Revenue Assumption & OpenAI Confirms IPO
- Why Customer Service, Defence and Robotics are Overinflated

My notes below:

1. We Are So Much More Addicted to Tokens Than We Think

As employees adopt 10 to 20 sub-agents running around the clock, businesses are facing unexpected $20,000 per-employee token bills. This is not a temporary trend. Token consumption is becoming an irreversible dependency, with top talent increasingly viewing continuous access to AI compute as essential to doing their jobs.

2. Why Customer Support Is Dead as a Category

Standalone customer support software is collapsing as agentic interfaces merge siloed tools into unified workflows. Legacy CS and CX platforms risk becoming cheap commodities as support capabilities are absorbed into cross-functional sales, marketing, and operational agents.

3. Why AI Services Companies Are a Bullshit Category

Funding traditional law or accounting firms rebranded as AI services companies relies on convoluted structures that look great on spreadsheets but break down in execution. Premium tech multiples cannot be created simply by wrapping overworked elite graduates in AI-powered agency business models.

4. $9 Billion Doesn’t Clear the Bar for Seed Investing in 2026

High seed valuations combined with massive dilution mean even multi-billion-dollar exits may no longer generate fund-returning outcomes. If effective entry pricing reaches $600 million after dilution, a $9 billion exit produces only a 15x return, far below the 50x outcomes that drive venture power laws.

5. If Danger Can Be Described as the Absence of Choice, They Were Now in Danger

As Anthropic gains enterprise share and improves profitability, OpenAI risks losing control over its public-market timeline. Massive capital requirements and intensifying competition across every model tier could leave it with fewer strategic options, forcing it to accept whatever valuation public markets are willing to offer.

6. It’s All About Code. That’s the Only Sentence That Matters

Coding is the highest-ROI, fastest-adapting, and most critical workload in AI. While consumer chat products struggle with low willingness to pay and heavy compute subsidies, developer workflows command massive enterprise budgets and offer a clearer path to durable software value creation.
